title: Excel: A Financial Modelling System
summary: Since the calculation engine of Excel was the subject of a major upgrade to accommodate Dynamic Arrays in 2018, there has been a series of seismic changes to the art of financial modelling. This paper will show the traditional financial modelling techniques for spreadsheets can be replaced by radically different approaches that have significant gains in readability, performance and flexibility. With so much power added to the Excel engine in recent years, it is the responsibility of financial modellers to ensure that they are building in the simplest and most auditable way possible going forward.

title: Grassmann: The Coordinate-Independent Linear Algebra Programming Language
summary: Scientists, engineers, and mathematicians often formulate algorithms using coordinate-independent linear algebra because its tools are composable and harder to misuse. For numerical processing, however, users must translate these ideas into coordinate-dependent array code. Most practitioners do so prematurely because tools such as NumPy lack coordinate-independent representations, while existing languages with such constructs do not model enough linear algebra for the situations where they matter. We propose Grassmann, a small language bridging coordinate-independent linear algebra and coordinate-dependent implementations. It uses dependent types, linear types, and partially (pseudo-)invertible computation to model situations arising in exterior algebra and differential geometry. It targets the linear algebra at a point on a manifold, a prerequisite for many specifications in scientific computing and computer graphics. A language for coordinates lets users move between these representations. We give a denotational semantics assigning meaning without coordinates and an operational semantics translating Grassmann to array code under a choice of coordinates. Our main metatheoretic result shows that operational evaluations agree with the denotational semantics under an arbitrary choice of coordinates. This models how practitioners translate linear algebra for computers and suggests an approach to algorithmic optimization at a high level of abstraction. Our optimized implementation generates code for exterior algebra operations with overheads no more than 10%.

title: Stochastic Summaries: Characterizing Structured Datasets Using Probabilistic Programs
summary: What does my data look like? We study the problem of representing and learning summaries of datasets that account for both their structural and statistical properties. This problem is widely useful across many application domains that involve large datasets and analysis/modeling of data, and is of particular interest to Programming Languages. In particular, in this work we focus on the problem of learning these "stochastic summaries" for tree-like data composed of inductive datatypes and argue that probabilistic programs over inductive datatypes can effectively represent the desired summaries. We present Tali, a Probabilistic Programming Language over inductive datatypes, and study the problem of learning such programs from data samples. We identify a semantic property, called Observation-Bounded Compilability, which identifies a set of recursive probabilistic programs which admit exact inference, and can represent many useful and complex probabilistic structures. We then propose an algorithm for learning Tali programs satisfying the OBC property from observations using a combination of program synthesis (stochastic search) and maximum likelihood inference. We implement our learning framework, evaluate it on a diverse benchmark suite, and record our observations on the merits of our approach. We demonstrate the utility of learning stochastic summaries as symbolically-represented priors for downstream learning tasks. We also showcase another utility by using our technique to learn operational profiles of real-world datasets.

title: MBUndo: Sound, Automatic, and Efficient Measurement-Based Uncomputation for Quantum Circuits
summary:
Quantum programs that use temporary values, known as \emph{ancilla} qubits, must explicitly \emph{uncompute} each ancilla back to zero to ensure that the program produces correct outputs. Conventional uncomputation uses unitary quantum gates, whereas leading quantum algorithms now leverage \emph{measurement-based uncomputation} (MBU), which replaces costly unitary $T$ gates with cheaper measurements and phase corrections.
  Current quantum programming frameworks can use measurement to uncompute specific gates such as Toffoli. No automatic transformation, however, accepts an arbitrary circuit whose ancillas are computed and uncomputed via the standard approach and converts the circuit to use MBU\@. Researchers instead apply MBU to individual circuit designs by hand, which limits algorithm development and compiler optimization.
  Such a transformation has not existed due to two fundamental unknowns: where MBU applies and which gates realize MBU for an arbitrary computation. To solve these, we first present a static analysis that identifies, for each ancilla qubit, each circuit position where measurement is sound --- subsuming basic assumptions that MBU only applies at the end of a circuit. Next, we present circuit transformations that soundly turn unitary uncomputation gates into efficient phase corrections after measurement --- generalizing rewrite rules from prior literature that are either limited to a single gate or not applicable to a general circuit.
  We present \textsf{MBUndo}, an integrated compiler pass that automatically converts circuits to measurement-based uncomputation. It requires no user annotations other than which qubits are ancillas, the same as needed by existing uncomputation synthesizers, and can enhance their output circuits. We evaluate \textsf{MBUndo} on 22 benchmarks to reveal \emph{T} gate reductions of ${>}36.5\%$ over uncomputation synthesizers.

title: Vectorizing Recurrences over Semirings
summary:
Recurrences are ubiquitous in signal and image processing, bioinformatics, numerical computing, combinatorial optimization, and many other domains. Because recurrences seem inherently sequential, they are often implemented serially and thus do not leverage vector instructions in modern hardware. This leaves much of the available, often highly parallel, hardware underutilized.
  In this paper, we present an algebra of recurrences over semirings and study algebraic identities that enable vectorization. Using our algebraic framework, we present a number of vectorizing transformations that yield efficient, vectorized implementations across various settings. These transformations naturally extend to 2D recurrences and mutual recurrences.
  We implement the recurrence algebra and the vectorizing transformations in a compiler called VecRec.VecRec compiles recurrence programs to efficient vectorized C++ implementations. The generated kernels can achieve up to an order-of-magnitude speedup over serial implementations across a wide variety of recurrences. A case study in bioinformatics shows that they are competitive with, and in many cases better than, existing libraries with manually-crafted vectorization.

title: Functional Logic Programming: Improving Logic Programs with Ease
comment: To appear in Theory and Practice of Logic Programming (TPLP)
summary: Logic programming is based on defining relations. Functions are often considered as syntactic sugar which can be transformed into predicates so that their logic is not used for computational purposes. In this paper, we show that the use of functions improves the operational behavior of logic programs without loosing the flexibility of logic programming. For this purpose, we present a systematic transformation from predicates and goals into functions and nested expressions, respectively. By evaluating functions in a demand-driven manner and taking potential failures into account, it is ensured that the execution of the transformed programs will never require more steps than the original programs but can decrease the number of steps---in the best case reducing infinite search spaces to finite ones. Thus, functional logic programming provides an adequate basis to improve the operational behavior of logic programs without changing their semantics. This also shows that, from an operational point of view, functional logic programming has clear advantages compared to relation-based logic programming.

title: Univalent Non-Associative Categorical Structures
summary: We study category-like structures in which composition is not associative, especially Munch-Maccagnoni's duploids, in univalent foundations. Included is a definition of what a univalent duploid is: one where isomorphisms of a suitable kind render the objects indistinguishable to the type theory. We show that the existing construction of a duploid from an adjunction is not univalent as a "single-sorted" duploid, and provide a novel construction which is. This work is formalized in the UniMath library for the Rocq proof assistant.

title: Coinduction in Grounded Arithmetic
summary: A grounded arithmetic counts a sentence as true only when a terminating process establishes it; a sentence no such process settles has no value. Such a logic can state that an event happens, but not that it never happens under unbounded choice. This paper extends such a logic so that it can. The base is Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) with Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA)'s least-fixed-point reading and ground induction. It adds a separate greatest-fixed-point former $ν$ with Park's coinduction rule, proves that one former cannot carry both ground induction and coinduction, and adds a dichotomy rule: the classical disjunction between a least-fixed-point atom and the greatest-fixed-point atom of its dual, under a derivable premise that the body's leaves are decided. The systems are sound for an explicit model reading every $ν$-body at its greatest fixed point, hence consistent; they agree with the least model wherever it has a value and prove sentences it leaves without one. The dichotomy replaces the underivable hypothesis that an order is well-founded by the derivable one that its steps are decided; the change of model pays for the move. With ground induction the dichotomy derives the omniscience rule of the sibling arithmetic OGA, so the system has no semantics whose certificates for universals are its own proofs. The systems prove, as single sentences, that every decided tree is well-founded or has an infinite branch given by a term, total in the new model; that random assignment terminates while its divergent twin runs forever; that a fair loop terminates and the alternating-bit protocol delivers every message; that open games are determined; that the termination gap in Nakata and Uustalu's trace semantics closes; and that Cinderella wins the bucket game at capacity three. Isabelle/HOL checks every result.

title: Blazing-Fast SMT-LIB Parsing for Rust and Lean
summary: SMT-LIB is a standard input format for Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers. However, parsing the format is non-trivial and can become a bottleneck, e.g. when retrieving benchmark metadata or normalising the input for solvers. We introduce blazing-smtlib, a Rust parsing library for SMT-LIB, and BSmtLib, its port to Lean. We outline the library API we designed for composability and extensibility (including non-standard SMT-LIB commands), and discuss our implementation decisions for fast lexing and parsing. We proved that our lexing and parsing with Lean-specific optimisations match our formalised reading of the SMT-LIB syntax. We measured performance on a representative sample from the 2025 SMT-LIB corpus and found that blazing-smtlib is more than 6 times faster on the geometric mean than previous parsing libraries and BSmtLib is faster or comparable to them.

title: VerusWeave: A Benchmark for Proof Repair in Concurrent Verus Programs
summary:
Concurrent software underpins critical infrastructure, including operating systems and databases, yet thread interactions can have bugs that bypass conventional testing. Verus extends Rust with formal verification capabilities, enabling developers to specify, implement and prove the correctness of concurrent code in the same language. Although coding agents have been explored for automated proof construction, existing Verus benchmarks offer limited coverage of concurrency-specific examples that connect atomic operations to abstract protocols.
  To address this gap, we introduce VerusWeave, the first benchmark dedicated to concurrent proof repair, derived from four open-source projects. It comprises 75 focused tasks and 17 full-module variants that exercise features used to verify low-level concurrent code. Tasks remove selected proof annotations and require agents to fill gaps, while preserving executable code and specifications. The evaluation harness validates repairs using Verus and a change checker, recording solutions, execution traces, and resource usage. An initial evaluation of four general-purpose coding-agent harnesses achieved 75-85% success on focused tasks and 29-47% on full-module variants, highlighting the challenge of autonomous module-wide repairs. VerusWeave provides a reusable foundation for evaluating automated proof construction for concurrent software.

title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale
summary: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.

title: Cartesian closedness of lax comma categories
summary: For a finitely complete category X, we prove that the lax comma category Cat//X is cartesian closed if and only if its free coproduct completion Fam(X) is cartesian closed. The proof uses a change-of-base theorem: postcomposition with a functor induces a left adjoint between lax comma categories precisely when that functor is a left multiadjoint. We describe the exponentials and derive examples from known results on family categories.

title: WFDB-x: Conformance-Tested Implementations of the WFDB Software Package in Seven Programming Languages
summary: The WFDB format is widely used to store and exchange physiological waveforms and annotations. However, existing software implementations are limited to C, Python, and MATLAB/Octave, can produce different results in corner cases and checksum calculations, and have defaults such as sampling frequency and gain, that can lead to silent misinterpretation of recordings. We developed WFDB-x, a cross-language, performance-optimized reimplementation of WFDB in seven programming languages, with extensive unit tests, to provide consistent WFDB processing across programming languages. We reimplemented the WFDB Software Package 10.7.0 natively in Python, C++, Rust, Julia, R, MATLAB/Octave, and Kotlin, using AI-assistance under human direction and review. Each implementation has library functions, a high-level interface, and command-line tools. We compared their outputs with those of the original C programs using 1098 conformance cases, 877 legacy-mode cases, unit tests, and differential fuzzing. Deliberate changes remove implicit waveform parameters, restrict file and network access, and prevent annotation loss. A legacy mode retains the original behavior. All seven implementations passed every conformance and legacy-mode case on the tested Linux platform, with matching outputs. The unit tests contain 9353 assertions. C++, Rust, and Julia read records 1.5-6.9 times faster than the original C library, while the Python implementation wrote records 9.2 times faster than the existing wfdb-python library in the benchmark. WFDB-x provides a tested, open-source basis for reading and writing physiological recordings consistently across seven languages, supporting reproducible research and software development without requiring a shared programming environment. We also share details of the AI-assisted development process and token utilization, which may be useful for other applications.

title: Extensible Programmatic Specification of Finite Element Methods
summary: Finite element methods (FEMs) are a powerful and ubiquitous tool for solving engineering problems. Experimenting with different finite elements can improve the quality and efficiency of solutions. In some cases, the wrong (but nonetheless most common) choice of finite element will produce solutions which converge to the wrong answer regardless of mesh resolution. However, in practice, the choice of finite element is not explored due to the complexity of re-deriving and re-implementing finite element methods. Trying a new finite element is challenging because practitioners must manually deduce formulas to use these elements and implement them within a potentially complex system. We address this problem by introducing ElementForge, a finite element system that is parametric over the literate mathematical specification of a finite element in a domain-specific language (DSL). The ElementForge compiler reasons about tensor spaces, tensors, and tensor bases from first principles to derive implementations of finite elements. The ElementForge compiler is able to automatically derive implementations of finite elements previously only derived by hand. Further, ElementForge minimally couples several key mathematical concepts, mainly tensor fields, mesh topologies, sparse tensors, and assembled finite element operators, to produce a complete finite element system that is parametric over the choice of element. Consequently, the elements derived by the compiler can be applied parametrically to new meshes, PDEs, and boundary conditions. We evaluate our system by implementing several simulations with different finite elements, demonstrating that our system can explore tradeoffs in generality, accuracy, speed, and representational complexity. For example, we are able to implement the Morley, Bell, Argyris, and Hermite like elements with less than 50 lines of code and use them all in a single simulation.
